accuracy.evidence: Wording checked against the English National Curriculum Years 3–4 writing composition statement (draft and write by composing and rehearsing sentences orally, including dialogue, progressively building a varied and rich vocabulary and an increasing range of sentence structures) and English Appendix 2 for Years 3–4 (conjunctions when, if, because, although; inverted commas to punctuate direct speech). Every dialogue line keeps the ! or ? inside the closing inverted comma and leaves the reporting clause outside, as in the Year 3 Appendix 2 examples.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the known Year 3 slips: inverted commas round the whole sentence including 'called Dad', a marks dot in the middle of the spoken words, a lively but wrong verb (stomped for a sneaking fox, yelled for a secret, whispered across a field), 'so' used where the clause is the reason, adjective piles treated as better writing, choppy repeated 'ran', and every sentence in the same shape.

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanism is oral rehearsal of alternatives: tap the gap dots to place opening and closing inverted commas, drop verbs into one slot and hear why each fits or not, drop a conjunction between two clauses, pick one of three versions of the same idea, and cycle each story line through short, joined and dialogue shapes until all three are used. It differs from flagoral (saying one sentence and counting words, ages 5–6), flagsent (building a complete sentence) and flagwhen (time and cause conjunctions); the 30% shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers each rule from feedback: tapping the dot before 'shouted' gives 'Tom did not say "shouted". Only the spoken words go inside'; dropping 'stomped' gives 'Stomping is loud. The fox would be heard and seen'; 'so' for the coat pair asks whether that version makes sense; the long owl version is rejected as an adjective pile. The step summaries then confirm the rule.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'Round the whole sentence' for the inverted commas is disproved when the reporting-clause dots are refused; 'The loudest, most exciting word' is disproved by stomped and yelled failing; 'The most describing words' is disproved when the adjective-pile version is rejected.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions, twelve tagged wrong-answer messages: marks round the reporting clause, marks round the wrong words, a loud verb for sneaking, a plain verb, 'so' for a reason, 'but' with no surprise, adjective pile, choppy repetition, writing faster instead of varying, adding more of the same, longer as the aim, and dropping full stops.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs pass the learner limit of FK 6.5 with short sentences and concrete examples (fox, Mia's coat, Tom shouting); canvas prompts are under ten words; young-class 56 px buttons. Adult text is within FK 9.5 and uses the exact terms composing and rehearsing sentences orally, dialogue, varied and rich vocabulary, sentence structures, conjunction, clause, inverted commas, direct speech and reporting clause.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler patterns and the 12% duplicate gate against every lesson, including Saying Sentences Before Writing Them, Building sentences and Expressing Time, Place and Cause. Each kid paragraph adds one idea (rehearse, try words, try shapes with conjunctions, dialogue and mix); adult paragraphs give the curriculum, why rehearsal works, the mistakes and the lab outline.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px Android light and iPhone 13 dark screenshots of all steps: the dialogue line with six tap dots fits one row, the verb and conjunction chips sit in four equal boxes, the three version cards wrap long lines onto two rows, and the three story rows show their shape label; every action also has a full-width button that wraps.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: every task completes with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge shows, axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in light and dark themes, and there are no console errors. Every canvas drag or tap has a button route (a button per inverted-comma gap, per verb, per conjunction, per version and per story line), and the canvas aria-label announces each result.

sources: Department for Education (2013), English programmes of study: key stage 2, Years 3–4 writing composition (statutory requirements)
Department for Education (2013), English Appendix 2: vocabulary, grammar and punctuation, Years 3 and 4 (conjunctions, inverted commas for direct speech)
